slides.title: The Auction House Narrative
slides.alt: Flow diagram. A customer, who has a job to get done, asks auction house A, which receives the job request. Auction house A and the outcomes sit in a frame labelled Ecosystem of auction houses. If A can handle the job, an arrow labelled no need to share leads to A handles the job, all credit to A. If A cannot handle it, an arrow leads to A auctions off the job request, where B, C and others bid; an arrow labelled B wins leads to B handles the job, credit shared by A and B. Under the frame: Common goal: as many served customers as possible.
slides.notes: To get their jobs handled, customers ask an auction house. If the auction house can handle the job itself, it keeps all the credit and involves no one else. If it cannot, it can still hope for part of the credit by auctioning off the job request to the other auction houses. The ecosystem of auction houses shares one goal: to serve as many customers as possible. That is why the auction houses of the six groups must interoperate.

slides.alt: Two graphs side by side. slides.title: Your Group and the Task Force Iterate
slides.alt: Loop diagram in two frames. Frame Your group: Argue for your role (arguments and demonstrators) and Implement (WebSub, MQTT, and your own ADRs). Frame Task force: Negotiate (delegates of all six groups) and Decide (one ADR per decision in the decision log). Arrows run clockwise: from Argue to Negotiate, labelled your delegate; from Negotiate to Decide, labelled may supersede earlier ADRs; from Decide to Implement, labelled cite its ADR in yours; from Implement back to Argue, labelled experience from the code.
slides.notes: Your delegate needs your support: arguments and demonstrators that strengthen their position in the negotiations. In your own ADRs, state how you implement a task force decision and cite its ADR, record the decisions your group takes on its own, and say where your role motivates a decision.

points: (b) every group VM reaches it at its public hostname or address, not at a private one
(c) a group other than its operator uses it in a demonstration
(d) if a group operates it, it runs on that group's VM or an extra VM from the course

slides.title: A Fallback

callout.text: Which components have no fallback yet among the provided instances?

paragraphs: Rule 9: a second counting instance of the same component
points: Groups use it alongside the first instance, or switch to it by changing configuration only

aside.alt: The same diagram with the answer in colour: the WebSub hub of Switchboard is green, and the MQTT broker of HiveMQ and the resource directory of the course are teal.

slides.notes: Answer to the question: the MQTT broker (only HiveMQ) and the discovery service (only the course's resource directory). The WebSub hubs have a fallback: Google and Switchboard, once both count. A group can give the broker a fallback, e.g. a broker on its own VM that another group uses. From Exercise 9, the pod server and the identity provider have no fallback either among the provided instances: only the course CSS provides them.
